tagline: Read a line. Look away. Say it back, then say what you make of it. All the way through a section.
task: Read each line, look away, say it back in your own words out loud, then react to it. At the end of every stimulus, give your Read.
rules: Everything here is done out loud. The whole section is recorded in one take, and it never pauses.
Read one line silently, with full intonation. Then press space.
Look away from the screen and say the line back in your own words. Then say what you make of it.
Press space again to move to the next line, or just stop talking and it moves on its own.
The moment the last line is coloured, give your Read of the whole stimulus. No gap.
Then straight into the next stimulus. No breaks, no checking anything, all the way to the end.

briefing.lede: This is the foundation the rest of your prep is built on, so it is worth reading this page properly once before you start.

sections.heading: You can understand every sentence and still arrive with nothing.
body: You follow a stimulus, sentence by sentence, and it all makes sense as it goes. Then you get down to answer choice C and realise you are holding almost none of it. That is not a comprehension problem. It is a retention problem, and it is the one this drill was built for.
Understanding is necessary for everything and sufficient for nothing. If the argument is not still with you while you work the answers, your understanding never gets the chance to help.

Most of what we call reading is optimised for one thing, which is getting to the end. Scanning for names. Dropping the connecting words. Turning a list of three into one label. Sliding over the long word you would rather not pronounce. That is a perfectly good way to read a phone bill. It is a bad way to read something that will ask you for every detail back.
You are not broken, and this is not a sign of anything. It is a habit you were taught, brought to the wrong fight. Habits get replaced.

sections.heading: What you actually do, per line.
body: Three beats, on one line at a time, all the way down the stimulus. Then a fourth once the stimulus is finished.

steps.label: Read it.
steps.body: Intake only. Information going in, nothing coming back out yet. Read it with full intonation so every word gets its weight, and take on about a sentence at a time. When you are unsure how much to take, take less. What gets lost when you take on too much is always the front of it.

steps.label: Say it back.
steps.body: Look away from the screen, or close your eyes, and say the line back in your own words, out loud, like you are telling a friend what it said. Out of order is fine. Casual is fine. Laughing is fine.

steps.label: Colour it.
steps.body: React. Say something back to the author. A doubt, a question, an example, a joke, a feeling. One or two seconds is plenty, and it does not have to be clever.

steps.label: Give your Read.
steps.body: Once the last line of the stimulus is coloured, say what the argument is actually doing and where it is vulnerable. Immediately, with no pause to compose it. This is the part that gets checked.

sections.heading: Look away. That part is on you.
body: Nothing on this screen hides. The whole stimulus stays readable the entire time, which means the only thing stopping you rereading a line while you say it back is you looking away from it.

That is deliberate, and it is how the method is taught. Reading while you recall is a one way street with cars coming both ways. It jams. You stop using your memory at all, and you slide straight back into the author's exact words instead of finding your own.

It is also the version that still works when you are not in this app. Looking away is a habit you can take to a paper section and to test day. A screen that hides the text for you is a crutch that cannot come with you.

sections.heading: Simpler is not the same as shorter.
body: Do not say back the gist, the summary, or the important parts. You cannot know which parts were important until after you have read the whole thing, so filtering on the way through mostly means quietly throwing out the piece you were going to need.
Fewer words is fine when the words genuinely cover the same ideas. Fewer ideas is not.

Two ways to feel the standard. One is a therapist reflecting you back: drop a single adjective and you can tell instantly that they were not really listening. The other is a job interview, where you repeat the task back to prove you could actually do it.

So keep the names, the numbers, the dates and the small connecting words that tell you how two ideas relate. Each one is its own detail, and none of them are safe to drop just because the sentence around them survived. Lists are the hardest case. Two items and you cope, three and your brain files them as one thing with no contents. Say each item with a different tone and they stay separate.

sections.heading: Colouring is what makes the rest of it real.
body: This is the beat people want to skip, and it is the one the whole drill turns on.

Here is where it came from. Watching a student say a stimulus back perfectly, every word correct, and every word coming out like an empty cardboard box. Right words, no music, no sense that he knew what was inside any of them. The fix was one extra instruction: say something about what you just read. Anything.

His reaction was not clever. It did not need to be. The empty box quality vanished, because you cannot react to something you have not actually understood. Your brain optimises away anything a process does not use, so a recall with nothing downstream of it quietly degrades into miming the right words. Requiring a reaction forces the understanding to be real.

There is a memory reason too. Memory files relationships, not items. Remembering four four four four four is easy because it is one relationship. Remembering eight four six two zero is five separate things. When you react to a line by pulling in something you already know, the new thing and the old thing fire together and wire together, and the new one is far more likely to survive to the answer choices. It is not better compression. It is better indexing.

One standard, and it is the only one. If your reaction could be pasted onto any other sentence on the test, it is not a reaction. Cool. Sounds good. I like this one. Those are placeholders. The moment you push on a claim, or notice what it quietly takes for granted, or connect it to something outside the page, you have started doing the question instead of waiting for it.

sections.heading: You will think you have nothing to say. Everybody does.
body: Two things are actually happening when you freeze.

The first is a private clock. You have a limit on how long a pause feels acceptable, and it is shorter than you think. If the rule were that you do not leave the chair until you say something, you would find something. You can.

The second is a word you are hiding from yourself. The real sentence is almost always that you cannot think of anything worthwhile to say. Judging a thought for quality before you let it exist is exactly what makes people decide they are not creative.

So say the mediocre one and do better on the next line. Movement is life here. If all you have is that you do not know what is going on, say that out loud rather than sitting in silence, and keep going.

When you are properly stuck: ask the text a question, then answer it yourself straight away. Do not leave the question hanging, because a bare question is usually just a rephrasing with a question mark on the end.

sections.heading: Does this not slow me down?
body: It costs a little on every line, and it buys back far more than it costs.

Think of a mile you have to cover in ten minutes. You can take the residential street at the limit with a few speed bumps, or the business highway with a one in ten chance of being pulled over, twenty five times in a row.

Colouring is the speed bump. Real, small, every time. The single biggest time sink on this test is not knowing the answer. Being down to B and D with no way to break the tie, even two or three times in a section, costs more than a whole section's worth of reacting.

And it pays back twice. Your Read arrives with no pause, because you have been analysing the whole way down instead of starting from cold at the end. And the answer choices get settled on evidence, because you still have a live memory of the argument to test them against instead of a coin flip.

sections.heading: Here is one done, start to finish.
body: A short stimulus, worked the way you are about to work twenty three of them. Notice that the reaction on the third line is the whole answer, and it turns up long before the argument is finished.

demo.caption: Opponents of peat harvesting argue it would alter the ecological balance of the country's peat rich wetlands, and that as a direct consequence much of the water supply would be threatened with contamination. But this cannot be true, because in Ireland, where peat has been harvested for centuries, the water supply has not been contaminated. So we can safely proceed with harvesting peat.

beats.text: Opponents of peat harvesting argue it would alter the ecological balance of the country's peat rich wetlands.
People who don't want peat harvested say that harvesting it would throw off the balance of these wetlands.
Which I assume matters, somehow. Go on.
And that as a direct consequence much of the water supply would be threatened with contamination.
And if that balance goes, the water supply could get contaminated.
Okay, that would actually be bad. That is a real reason not to do it.
But this cannot be true, because in Ireland, where peat has been harvested for centuries, the water supply has not been contaminated.
The author says no, that cannot be right, because Ireland has harvested peat for hundreds of years and their water is fine.
But what if we are not Ireland?
So we can safely proceed with harvesting peat.
So go ahead and harvest the peat.
No. What if we are not Ireland? The whole thing rests on us being enough like a different country for their result to carry over, and nothing here says we are.

sections.heading: React freely. Save the editing for The Read.
body: Colour with no filter on the way down and let it be messy. Then be the editor once, at the end of the stimulus.

That split matters because The Read is the part with an answer key. If you are vetting every reaction as it forms, you slow down, you say less, and the good ones never get out. If you have been reacting honestly the whole way, your Read is usually already sitting there. Often it is the last thing you just said.
So do not stop and compose one. Say it the instant the last colour lands.

sections.heading: Twenty minutes, and what that number actually means.
body: The goal is twenty minutes for the whole section. With a fifty three minute accommodation it is twenty five, and with seventy minutes it is thirty.

It only counts if you read, said back, coloured and gave a Read on every stimulus. Beating the clock with three of them skipped is not beating the clock, and this checks the condition, not just the time.
There is no clock on the screen while you work, on purpose. A timer in the corner is what produces the rushed, skating read this drill exists to fix. It is measured quietly and you see it at the end.
Expect your first one to take a long time. Somewhere near fifty minutes is normal, and it is not a bad sign. You get faster the way runners get faster, which is by running more, not by hurrying.

sections.heading: One a day holds you steady. The second one is where you improve.
body: Do at least three of these back to back, and six if you can manage it. No breaks between them, and no reviewing between them.
One drill a day will keep your skill roughly where it is. The improvement starts on the second consecutive one, which is the whole reason the number matters.
Review is its own sitting, later. If you check your work between sections you stop drilling and start scorekeeping, and the next section gets run by whoever is reacting to that number.

sections.heading: What this is doing while you work.
body: It records the whole section in one unbroken take and never pauses, because the timing only means something if nothing was stopped. It transcribes what you actually said, word for word, so your Read can be checked against the key without you having to write anything down as you go.
It will not interrupt you, speak to you, or mark anything while you are inside the section. Nothing appears until the section is over.
That is not the app being quiet for the sake of it. Anything that grades you mid section teaches you to vet a thought before you say it, and that is the exact habit colouring exists to break.

briefing.closer: Expect the first one to run long and to feel clumsy out loud. That is what this feels like while it is working.

coach.drill: a whole Logical Reasoning section run out loud, where the student reads each line of a stimulus, looks away, says it back from memory in her own words, reacts to it, and gives a Read of the whole stimulus before moving to the next one
rubric: Judge by meaning, never by wording. Her own words are required here, so a good recall will never match the line's phrasing. High overlap with the original is the failure, not the standard.
Order is free. She is encouraged to deliver the ideas out of the order she read them in, and reordering must never cost her anything.
Casual, unpolished, laughing delivery is expected. Never mark down for style, length or fluency.
A detail merely gestured at is not carried. Naming the topic is not the same as saying what was claimed about it.
Numbers, names, dates, quantities and connecting words are each their own detail. Never treat one as carried because the sentence around it was.
A reaction that could be pasted onto any other sentence does not count as a colour. Judge whether it engages this content, never whether it is correct or well put.
Score The Read against the captured key for that stimulus, not against a retelling. A different name for the same move is fine; missing the move is not.
Silence during a silent read is correct and expected. Only silence inside a recall or a colour counts against her.
coach.partial_rule: Mark 'partial' when the retelling is real but at least one detail went missing, which is the drill's ordinary state. Mark 'incorrect' only when the response is a gist or a topic label rather than a retelling.
